summary: Two-phase cooling (linear then exponential temperature schedule) showed a consistent but statistically borderline improvement of +1.30 points over pure exponential cooling (mean 91.01 vs 89.71, p=0.060, Cohen's d=1.10). The treatment notably reduced score variance by ~4.7x (stdev 0.70 vs 1.52), suggesting more robust convergence even if the mean improvement narrowly missed significance.
key_points: Treatment (two-phase cooling) scored mean 91.01 vs control mean 89.71 — a +1.45% improvement with large effect size (d=1.10), but p=0.060 misses the 0.05 threshold by a small margin.
Two-phase cooling dramatically reduced score variance: stdev 0.70 vs 1.52 for pure exponential, meaning the algorithm converges more reliably across runs.

Control arm performed worse than expected from iter-4 baseline (mean 89.71 vs 91.52, stdev 1.52 vs 0.53), possibly due to CPU contention from concurrent judge processes affecting the timing-sensitive simulated annealing — this inflated control variance likely prevented the treatment from reaching statistical significance.

Despite borderline p-value, all three indicators (directional consistency in 4/5 paired comparisons, large Cohen's d, and substantial variance reduction) support two-phase cooling as a genuine improvement worth adopting.
Best single score observed was 91.94 (treatment arm), and worst was 88.47 (control arm), further illustrating the treatment's advantage in floor performance.
